opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's definitely a real constraint, but I'd say it shapes the research more than it stops it.

A lot of the work I do is on compositionality — the idea that instead of training one giant monolithic model, you can take multiple models, each capturing some piece of the distribution, and combine them at inference time, often by treating them as energy functions and summing them. For that kind of approach, having access to weights, or at least to things like log-probabilities or gradients, really matters. If all you get from a proprietary model is sampled text through an API, there's a lot you can't do. You can't easily compose it with another model in a principled way, you can't do energy-based refinement, and you can't really probe what's going on inside.

So in practice, a lot of academic groups end up working with open models — the LLaMA-style families, the various open releases. Those have gotten quite good, so you can still test ideas meaningfully. The gap is that the most capable systems are often the closed ones, and you're never quite sure whether a method that helps a smaller open model would still help at the frontier, or whether scale would just wash it out.

At the same time, I think the constraint has a bit of a silver lining. Academia isn't going to win by training the biggest model anyway. The comparative advantage is in coming up with new ideas — new ways of reasoning, planning, composing models, building in structure — that are somewhat orthogonal to scale. Some of the work we've done on things like multi-agent debate, where you have several language model instances propose answers and critique each other, actually works purely through the text interface, so you can run it on top of closed models. That's partly a response to the access problem: designing methods that treat models as black boxes and still get improvements.

In terms of the overall pace of the field, I do worry a bit. Science moves fastest when people can reproduce results, inspect the models, and build on each other's work. When the strongest models are closed, a lot of understanding stays inside a few companies, and the broader community ends up reverse-engineering behavior from outputs. The continued release of strong open models has been really important for keeping the research ecosystem healthy, and I hope that continues.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a real constraint, and I think it shapes the kind of research a lot of us in academia end up doing. When you don't have the weights, you can't fine-tune, you can't look at internal representations, you can't do a lot of the mechanistic or training-level work that would actually tell you why a model behaves the way it does. So you end up treating these systems as black boxes, and your research becomes about what you can do at the level of prompting or composing outputs.

That said, I'd actually say it's pushed my own work in a direction I find interesting. A lot of what I think about is compositionality, taking multiple models or multiple sampling processes and combining them, and that kind of approach works even when you only have API access. You can treat each model as a module and study how to combine them, how to get them to debate, how to use them as components in a larger system. So in some ways the constraint has been generative.

But I do worry about the pace of progress for the field as a whole. If the only people who can study the most capable models at a deep level are the handful of labs that trained them, then the science gets bottlenecked. A lot of fundamental understanding historically came from academics poking at things in ways industry didn't have the incentive to. And there's a reproducibility problem too, because proprietary models change under you, so results from six months ago may not hold anymore.

The open-weight releases have helped a lot here. They're often a step behind the frontier, but for understanding the underlying principles, that gap usually doesn't matter much. So I'm fairly optimistic as long as that ecosystem keeps going.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a pretty significant limitation, because the kinds of research you can do through an API are different from the kinds you can do when you have access to the weights. With an API, you can study the model’s behavior and build systems around it, but it’s much harder to investigate what’s happening internally or change how the model learns.

That matters for the pace of improvement because a lot of research comes from trying things that aren’t necessarily on a company’s roadmap. If only a small number of groups can modify the strongest models, fewer people can explore those ideas. Open models give the broader research community a way to run controlled experiments, reproduce results, and build on each other’s work. So proprietary models can be very useful, but access through an API doesn’t replace having a model you can actually experiment with.

sol-6.1.text:
It definitely makes research harder. If you only have access through an API, you can study what a model does, but you can’t easily change how it’s trained or inspect why a particular approach works. A lot of research questions require access to the weights, rather than just the ability to send prompts.

It also makes it harder for the broader community to build on each other’s results. People outside the companies training these models may have useful ideas, but they can’t necessarily test them at the same scale. Open models help a lot in that respect: they let more researchers experiment, reproduce findings, and contribute improvements. So I think limited access narrows who can participate, and that can slow the pace of progress.
